messages.text: Bit of an oddball context — I have a lobster allergy specifically (not all shellfish, I tolerate shrimp and crab fine). Anyway, I'm trying to figure out retirement planning and feeling totally lost.

Noted on the lobster — and welcome to the club of people retirement-confused. Let me ask the questions any planner would: are you working with an employer 401k, do you have or have access to an IRA (traditional or Roth), what's your rough timeline, and do you have any meaningful debt apart from a mortgage?
401k with 4% employer match, no IRA yet, target retirement around age 65 (I'm 38), and a mortgage I'm 8 years into of a 30-year.

Solid starting point. The standard priority order most fee-only advisors would suggest:

1. **Contribute to your 401k up to the employer match.** That's free money — never leave it.
2. **Build a 3-6 month emergency fund** in a high-yield savings account, separate from investments.
3. **Open a Roth IRA** and max it if you can ($7,000/year for 2026, $8,000 if you're 50+). Tax-free growth and withdrawals in retirement is hugely valuable for someone with a 27-year horizon.
4. **Increase 401k contributions toward the annual max** ($23,000 for 2026). Pre-tax now, taxable in retirement.
5. **Don't rush the mortgage payoff** — at current rates if your mortgage is below ~5%, you mathematically come out ahead investing the difference.
OK so I'm doing #1 but not #2 or #3. Need to fix that.

That's a really common spot. The emergency fund is genuinely the highest priority — without it, a surprise expense forces you to either pull from retirement accounts (tax penalty) or take on high-interest debt. Start with 1 month of expenses parked at a high-yield account paying 4-5% and build from there over a few months.
Will do. Roth IRA — Fidelity? Vanguard? Schwab?

All three are essentially interchangeable for a Roth IRA. Pick whichever has the cleanest UX for you — they all offer free trades, no minimums, and zero-expense-ratio index funds. If you're starting from scratch with no existing relationships: Fidelity is probably the most beginner-friendly app right now.
